newsitem.title: USA: Key lawmakers changing Medicare means-test plan.
newsitem.headline: Key lawmakers changing Medicare means-test plan.

text.p: Key senators Monday backed off a controversial plan to make wealthier Medicare recipients pay more for doctors' care, saying they would instead push to make affluent seniors pay higher monthly premiums.

Both approaches are highly controversial, but the first was criticised as a "sick tax" that would have mainly affected those with medical problems. Sponsors said the premium plan was more equitable because it was based only on income.

As Congress began debate on massive budget legislation, its own analysts also estimated the House version of the budget bill, designed to expand health care to as many as 5 million uninsured children, would fall far short of that goal.

Congressional aides said senators had decided they did not have enough support for their original Medicare plan, which for the first time would have made wealthy seniors meet higher deductibles before Medicare coverage kicked in.
Their alternative, to be offered as early as Tuesday in the Senate, would increase the monthly $43.80 Medicare premium for well-off seniors.
"The important thing is a victory for the fairness idea, meaning no subsidies for those who don't need them," said a Democratic aide. "There appears to be broader support ... for the premium."
The idea of tying Medicare coverage to income is highly controversial and it was unclear whether the lawmakers would have the votes for the premium alternative.
"I'm opposed to both," said Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy, vowing to fight such proposals on the floor.
The Senate Monday opened debate on broad legislation cutting Medicare by $115 billion and Medicaid by about $13.6 bilion over five years.

The measure, and a companion House bill, also include $16 billion for children's health insurance and about $10 billion to restore cuts in welfare. The bills are needed to implement a five-year budget deal between Congress and the White House.
Aside from the deductible, fights are expected over Senate provisions raising the Medicare eligibility age to 67 from 65 and charge seniors $5 for home health visits.
Medicare Part B is voluntary, but nearly all eligible seniors choose it as it covers doctor, laboratory, outpatient hospital and other services not provided by the regular Medicare programme.

The current deductible is $100 per year and the monthly premium is $43.80. Seniors' monthly payment reflects only a quarter of the actual programme cost. The federal government subsidises the remaining 75 percent.
Under the original Senate bill, seniors with incomes $50,000 and above and couples with incomes $75,000 and above would have faced sharply higher out-of-pocket costs.
The deductible would have risen to about $500 a year at the $50,000/$75,000 income level, climbing to about $2,000 for individuals making more than $100,000 and couples making more than $125,000.

Under the amendment, the federal premium subsidy would diminish based on income. The phase-out would begin at $50,000/$75,000 and end at $100,000/$125,000. Seniors in the highest income bracket would pay about $2,160 in premiums.

Nebraska Democratic Sen. Robert Kerrey sponsored the original amendment. After criticism that the deductible plan amounted to a "sick tax" that would be difficult to administer, Kerrey altered his position.

On children's health, the House bill gives states $14.4 billion in block grants over five years to design their own insurance programmes. Republican leaders have said the goal was to cover up to half the nation's 10 million uninsured children.

The CBO estimated the number of children newly insured would be in the range of 500,000 a year, saying governors would spend part of the block grant money on direct health services or to make up for planned federal cuts in the Medicaid programme.

Opponents of block grants called on Republicans to come up with a better plan. "The children's health money should not be robbed," said Marian Wright Edelman, executive director of the Children's Defence Fund. "This is not there for governors to solve all their other kinds of state problems."
